node-1.label: A 27-year-old woman presented with elevated hepatobiliary enzymes

node-2.label: Patient occasionally drank alcohol and had no history of viral hepatitis, steatohepatitis, autoimmune liver disease, or metabolic liver disease.

node-3.label: Patient was taking axitinib, azelnidipine, and tramadol hydrochloride; after stopping alcohol and axitinib, her hepatobiliary enzyme levels remained unchanged.

node-4.label: Physical examination revealed no specific findings.

why.why: Liver biopsy showing PAX8-positive malignant cells within Glisson's capsule and occluding interlobular veins, plus CT/MRI hilar hypointensity, is interpreted by both the pathologist and radiologist as excluding drug-induced liver injury; enzymes also remained unchanged after stopping alcohol and axitinib. This reduces confidence to 0.02.

The cholestatic pattern initially suggested biliary disease, but biopsy-proven PAX8-positive malignant infiltration and the pathologist/radiologist analyses explicitly exclude primary biliary disease, attributing the bile duct changes to the malignant process. Confidence is lowered to 0.05.

Liver biopsy demonstrating PAX8-positive malignant cells within Glisson's capsule and occluding interlobular veins, CT/MRI hilar hypointensity, and expert confirmation of hepatic malignant infiltration provide definitive evidence of an occult hepatic malignant process. This explains the cholestatic enzyme profile and imaging abnormalities, so confidence is raised to 0.97.

node-12.label: Liver biopsy shows inflammatory bile duct destruction

node-13.label: CT/MRI reveals hypointensity in the hilar region on hepatobiliary phase

node-14.label: Hepatic malignant infiltration (PAX8-positive) is the underlying occult process

why.why: Biopsy-proven PAX8-positive malignant cells in Glisson's capsule and interlobular veins, with CT/MRI hilar hypointensity, are explicitly confirmed by the pathologist and radiologist as hepatic malignant infiltration, excluding drug injury and primary biliary disease. Confidence is increased to 0.95.

node-15.label: The PAX8-positive hepatic malignancy is of metastatic origin from an occult primary tumor

why.why: The pathologist and radiologist both interpret the PAX8-positive hepatic malignant infiltration as a metastatic process from an occult primary, and the biopsy findings are consistent with metastatic malignancy rather than primary hepatic tumor. Confidence is increased to 0.75.

node-16.label: Metastatic renal cell carcinoma (PAX8-positive) from an occult renal primary

why.why: Both the pathologist and radiologist identify PAX8 positivity as classically pointing to renal cell carcinoma, and the biopsy confirms PAX8-positive malignant cells in the liver. They recommend dedicated renal imaging, CD10/CAIX staining, and urinalysis to confirm the occult renal primary, raising confidence to 0.7 while the primary site remains unconfirmed.

node-17.label: Metastatic Müllerian/ovarian carcinoma (PAX8-positive) from an occult gynecologic primary

why.why: Although PAX8 is also expressed in Müllerian/ovarian carcinomas and the patient is a young woman, the expert analyses prioritize renal cell carcinoma as the most likely PAX8-positive primary and recommend renal evaluation first. Without gynecologic-specific evidence, confidence is lowered to 0.25.

node-18.label: Metastatic thyroid carcinoma (PAX8-positive) from an occult thyroid primary

attrs.why: Thyroid follicular-derived carcinomas are PAX8-positive and can present with hepatic metastases from an occult primary. This candidate refines the current frontier by suggesting thyroid ultrasound and TTF-1/thyroglobulin immunostaining.

node-19.label: Metastatic pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (PAX8-positive) from an occult pancreatic primary

attrs.why: Some pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors express PAX8 and can metastasize to the liver while remaining occult. This less common but plausible candidate refines the frontier further by prompting DOTATATE-PET/CT and chromogranin/synaptophysin staining.

node-21.label: Pathologist and radiologist recommend dedicated renal imaging, CD10/CAIX staining, and urinalysis to identify the occult primary
